abstract: Shrub encroachment can alter forage resources, soil–water processes, and landscape configuration in alpine grasslands, yet annual mapping remains challenging because shrub and herbaceous canopies converge spectrally and many apparent changes occur in diffuse ecotones. We developed a 10-m annual mapping framework integrating Sentinel-2 phenology, Sentinel-1 synthetic aperture radar (SAR) time-series information, and topographic covariates to distinguish shrubland from grassland in Maqu County on the northeastern Tibetan Plateau from 2018 to 2024. A learned SAR-derived shrubland-grassland discrimination score (SGDS) was constructed from annual Sentinel-1 descriptors using least absolute shrinkage and selection operator (LASSO)-regularized logistic regression to improve shrubland-grassland discrimination. In the 2024 benchmark experiment, the selected random forest (RF) configuration reduced classification error by approximately 17% relative to optical-only RF. SGDS outperformed the tested conventional SAR indices and the full SAR-statistics feature set, and adding SGDS increased RF accuracy from 91.26% to 92.47%. When the selected workflow was applied independently to each mapping year, annual overall accuracies ranged from 91.6% to 95.8%, based on the same 500 temporally screened reference locations spatially separated from the model-development samples. Nominal mapped shrubland area increased from 392.3 km2 in 2018 to 648.2 km2 in 2022 before declining to 560.4 km2 in 2024. Confidence and boundary-sensitivity analyses showed that the pronounced 2020–2021 increase was largely associated with low-confidence ecotonal pixels and decreased from + 96.91 to + 6.09 km2 as the mapped-class confidence threshold increased from 0.60 to 0.80, whereas the 2022–2024 decline remained negative under all tested confidence and boundary screens. Mapped shrubland area showed an apparent positive association with annual mean temperature, but this relationship was not robust after detrending and should be considered preliminary given the seven-year record. Overall, integrating learned SAR structural information with optical phenology improved annual shrubland-grassland mapping and provided a more reliable basis for interpreting mapped dynamics, with potential for locally calibrated application in comparable alpine regions.

title: Adapting medical vision foundation models for volumetric medical image segmentation via active learning and selective semi-supervised fine-tuning
abstract: Medical vision foundation models (Med-VFMs) have shown strong potential for medical image analysis by leveraging representations learned from large-scale self-supervised pre-training on unlabeled data. However, their performance and generalization remain limited in downstream tasks, particularly volumetric medical image segmentation. Although fine-tuning on labeled target-domain data improves performance, existing approaches typically rely on randomly selected samples, which may overlook informative data and hinder adaptation. To address this, we propose an Active Selective Semi-supervised Fine-tuning (ASSFT) framework for efficient adaptation of Med-VFMs to volumetric segmentation tasks. ASSFT integrates active learning with selective semi-supervised learning to maximize performance under limited annotation budgets without requiring source data. Specifically, we introduce an Active Test-Time Sample Query strategy that identifies informative target-domain samples using two complementary metrics: Diversified Knowledge Divergence (DKD) and Anatomical Segmentation Difficulty (ASD). DKD captures both the knowledge gap between pre-training and target domains and intra-domain diversity, enabling selection of samples containing novel and diverse information. ASD estimates segmentation difficulty by measuring predictive uncertainty in foreground regions, prioritizing anatomically complex cases over background-dominated samples. Furthermore, we propose a Selective Semi-supervised Fine-tuning strategy that leverages unlabeled data by incorporating only reliable pseudo-labeled samples based on predictive confidence and semantic proximity to labeled data, thereby mitigating noise. Extensive experiments on five volumetric segmentation tasks demonstrate that ASSFT consistently outperforms state-of-the-art active learning and domain adaptation methods while requiring substantially fewer annotations, highlighting its effectiveness, efficiency, and strong generalization capability.

title: Drift-aware denoising-uniform step optimization for fast diffusion sampling
abstract: Diffusion Probabilistic Models (DPMs) achieve strong generation quality, yet their inference remains expensive due to the large number of Neural Function Evaluations (NFEs). While recent acceleration methods mainly improve ODE solvers, time-step optimization is still largely driven by heuristic schedules and training-time error surrogates. In particular, existing objectives often neglect exposure bias during sampling, where local prediction errors are recursively amplified along the reverse trajectory. To address this gap, we introduce a reverse-time drift-aware surrogate objective for time-step optimization by incorporating a path-sensitivity profile that characterizes the accumulated reverse-time influence of local prediction residuals along the sampling trajectory. Building on this objective, we propose a Denoising-Uniform initialization mechanism that allocates steps uniformly in a cumulative denoising-difficulty coordinate and provides a denoising-aware starting point for subsequent optimization. This two-stage formulation refines step placement with a normalized combination of drift-sensitive and training-error profiles while keeping the pretrained model, solver, and NFE budget fixed. Extensive experiments on both generative sampling and inverse problems demonstrate consistent gains over strong baselines under matched solver and NFE settings. For example, on unconditional CIFAR-10, our method achieves an FID of 3.86 with only 15 NFEs.

title: Learning brain network states for neurological disorders via Koopman dynamics
abstract: Extracting discriminative and mechanistically interpretable representations from complex brain activity remains a fundamental challenge in neuroimaging-based diagnosis. Existing approaches typically rely on static functional connectivity, or on window-wise aggregation without explicit decomposition of nonlinear dynamics, limiting their ability to capture the evolution of intrinsic brain dynamics. Moreover, multimodal information and population structure are often modeled independently, restricting the exploitation of inter-subject relationships. In this work, we propose a unified framework, BrainDMNet, which integrates multimodal learning, population graph inference, and site-adversarial domain adaptation, with KoopmanEvoNet as the core dynamical modeling module. KoopmanEvoNet is a Koopman-based spiking neural network (SNN) that maps nonlinear brain dynamics into a latent operator space. It combines learned linear state evolution with sparse spike encoding to obtain compact dynamical representations. On this basis, a phenotype-guided multimodal population graph is constructed, where dynamical features, functional connectivity, and non-imaging attributes are fused via cross-modal attention, and inter-subject relationships are modeled through graph propagation. A site-adversarial domain adaptation strategy is introduced to mitigate cross-site distribution shifts. Experiments demonstrate that BrainDMNet improves classification performance compared with existing methods. More importantly, empirical analysis reveals that Koopman-derived dynamical features can amplify inter-group differences, with effect sizes increasing from small or moderate levels to large levels. These differences are not consistently reflected in global dynamical statistics, but are localized in specific Koopman modes and brain regions, indicating that neurodevelopmental disorders may involve localized alterations in brain dynamics rather than uniform global dynamical disruption.

title: Adversarial contrastive multi-view clustering via representation enhancement guided by reconstruction
abstract: Deep multi-view clustering (DMVC) learns unified and discriminative representations from multiple views to reveal consistent clustering structures. However, existing DMVC methods face two challenges: (1) many operate directly on original views, making learning highly dependent on view quality and limited by the information in the inputs; (2) contrastive learning methods for DMVC usually rely on batch negatives, which are not sufficiently challenging and thus provide limited guidance for learning discriminative decision boundaries. To address these issues, we propose ACRE-MVC, an adversarial contrastive multi-view clustering framework with adaptive representation enhancement guided by reconstruction. The reconstruction error is used as a relative cue to indicate how well the current latent representation preserves the structural information of each view, and this cue guides the construction of an enhanced latent representation that complements the original views. The enhanced representation is trained jointly with the original views under reconstruction and contrastive objectives, improving consistency learning. In addition, a generator synthesizes view-specific hard negatives to strengthen discriminability, while distribution alignment preserves semantic coherence across views. Extensive experiments on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of ACRE-MVC in improving clustering performance. The code is available at https://github.com/anhuiyanglihao/ACRE_MVC .

title: Exploring backdoor attack and defense algorithms in LLMS: Enhancing in-context learning security
abstract: In-context learning, a paradigm bridging the gap between pre-training and fine-tuning, has demonstrated high efficacy in several NLP tasks, especially in few-shot settings. Despite being widely applied, in-context learning is vulnerable to malicious attacks. In this work, we raise security concerns regarding this paradigm. Our studies demonstrate that an attacker can manipulate the behavior of large language models (LLMs) by poisoning the demonstration context, without the need for fine-tuning the model. Specifically, we design a new backdoor attack method, named ICLAttack , to target large language models based on in-context learning. Our method encompasses two types of attacks: poisoning demonstration examples and poisoning demonstration prompts, which can make models behave in alignment with predefined intentions. ICLAttack does not require additional fine-tuning to implant a backdoor, thus preserving the model’s generality. Crucially, we also explore a novel defense algorithm named ICLDefense aimed at ICLAttack, which utilizes model ensembles to defend against backdoor attacks. ICLDefense employs a lightweight auxiliary model to refine the outputs of LLMs through an ensemble-based strategy, achieving significant efficiency and scalability. Extensive experimental results across several language models, ranging in size from 1.3B to 180B parameters, demonstrate the effectiveness of our attack method, exemplified by a high average attack success rate of 95.0% across the three datasets on OPT models. Moreover, our ICLDefense algorithm substantially reduces the attack success rate compared to existing methods, while preserving model performance on the same settings.

title: GUARD-net: A geostationary satellite-based network for near-real-time active fire detection under class imbalance
abstract: Deep learning has substantially advanced satellite-based wildfire monitoring; however, near-real-time detection using geostationary satellite sensors remains challenged by severe class imbalance and domain shift across regions and satellite platforms. This study presents GUARD-Net, a geostationary satellite-based network for near-real-time active fire detection under class imbalance that integrates spectral, spatial, and topographic information within a convolutional framework. The model employs a bottleneck residual (BR) architecture together with focal loss (FL) to enhance sensitivity to rare fire pixels under highly imbalanced conditions. To enhance transferability, we introduce a heterogeneous-features weighted domain adaptation (HWDA) strategy, which aligns deep mixed features and shallow physical attributes (spectral/spatial/topographic) with a dynamic self-adaptive loss weighting scheme. Ablation experiments using Himawari-8/9 and Geostationary Operational Environmental Satellite-16 (GOES-16) data under controlled imbalance scenarios show consistent performance gains over baseline models. In baseline tests with a fire:non-fire ratio greater than 1:20, GUARD-Net attains F1 score > 0.94, Area Under the Precision-Recall Curve (PR-AUC) > 0.98, and Map-level Image Classification Efficacy (MICE) > 0.93; in a controlled sensitivity analysis with a prescribed 0.1% false-positive rate among non-fire samples, the 1:1000 tests yielded F1 score > 0.77, PR-AUC > 0.86, and MICE >0.71. Under the oracle checkpoint-selection protocol used for the six cross-domain transfer tasks, HWDA achieved unsupervised F1 score up to 0.955 (maintaining F1 = 0.863 with 10% unlabeled target data) and supervised F1 score up to 0.989 (reaching F1 score = 0.943 with 20% labeled target samples), with relative performance varying by transfer task and metric. Across 30 documented events from 2023, GUARD-Net detected 29 events; processing of the evaluated regional scenes required 2.5–3.9 min on the tested workstation, while comparisons with operational fire products varied by region. The results indicate that topographic inputs, focal-loss training, and heterogeneous-feature alignment can contribute to robustness across the evaluated terrain, class-imbalance, and domain-shift settings, supporting near-real-time wildfire detection from geostationary satellite observations.

title: Large-scale landslide susceptibility mapping via deep learning: A case study of Pakistan
abstract: Landslide hazards are highly abrupt and extremely destructive, posing a severe threat to global geological security. Landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) is a critical technology for reducing geological hazards, yet current methods still exhibit shortcomings in large-scale spatial modeling and the reliability assessment of results. In this study, an integrated pixel-based framework for large-scale LSM was developed and applied to the entire territory of Pakistan (880,000 km 2 ) using 20 landslide conditioning factors (LCFs) grouped into six categories. We implemented difference-weighted stratified sampling (DWSS) for training-negative selection, and adopted the LandslideNet model integrated with the spatial perception block (SPB) and dynamic channel squeeze-and-excitation (DCSE) module to conduct spatial correlation modeling. The challenge of large-scale computing was addressed via a multi-level block division and combination strategy, and the multi-stride median fusion (MSMF) algorithm was developed to achieve seamless merging of sub-blocks. The proposed framework generated the first 100 m national landslide susceptibility map for Pakistan. Under five-fold spatially contiguous regional hold-out evaluation, LandslideNet achieved the highest ROC-AUC (93.62 ± 3.41%) and PR-AUC (94.22 ± 4.17%) among the benchmark models, together with an F1-score of 89.07 ± 5.67%. The resulting susceptibility surface reveals a pronounced national spatial gradient, with high susceptibility concentrated in the northern mountains, more dispersed susceptible terrain across the western ranges, and predominantly low susceptibility over the southeastern plains. SBAS-InSAR analysis further showed the strongest deformation–susceptibility correspondence for LandslideNet among the evaluated models. SHAP analysis identified elevation and slope as the dominant contributors to model predictions, followed by distance to roads, temperature, and lithology. These results demonstrate the value of integrating established techniques for national-scale landslide susceptibility assessment and provide detailed susceptibility information for regional hazard screening and infrastructure planning. The code is available at https: // github.com/Trifurs/LandslideNet .

title: HotSAM: A Hotspot-Spatial-Adaptive Multi-Resolution framework for efficient long-term deformation monitoring in terrestrial radar interferometry
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Long-term deformation monitoring using ground-based interferometric radar (GBIR) inherently generates massive datasets. Current full-resolution processing paradigms face severe computational and storage bottlenecks, primarily because they expend equal resources on vast stable areas and localized deformation zones. To overcome this redundancy, this study proposes HotSAM (Hotspot-Spatial-Adaptive Multi-resolution), a novel framework that shifts from the conventional “one-size-fits-all” approach to a resource-adaptive strategy. The framework employs a two-stage processing scheme that first rapidly delineates active deformation zones using low-resolution analysis and an enhanced deformation hotspot detection algorithm. This allows for computationally intensive, fine-resolution processing to be selectively applied only where necessary. Beyond efficiency, the framework incorporates a joint error estimation model designed to simultaneously decouple instrument repositioning errors from atmospheric phase screens (APS), ensuring robust time-series analysis in discontinuous monitoring campaigns. In addition, a phase-matching geocoding approach is developed to establish geographic mapping of the radar-derived deformation products without requiring dedicated external ground control points. Extensive validation using both simulated and real-world GPRI-II datasets demonstrates the framework’s superior performance. Compared to traditional workflows, HotSAM achieves a 73.04 % reduction in processing time and a 96.95 % reduction in storage requirements, while maintaining high consistency in deformation results with only sub-millimeter deviations (i.e., 0.79 mm). Furthermore, quantitative sensitivity analysis of key parameters, including multi-look factors and deformation gradients, provides operational guidelines for optimal deployment. HotSAM offers a scalable, high-efficiency solution for long-term geohazard monitoring and establishes a potential blueprint for big-data processing in future terrestrial applications.

title: A spatially-adaptive automated sample generation framework via multi-source phenological fusion for large-scale crop mapping: demonstrated on peanuts in Shandong, China
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Accurate regional-scale crop mapping is critical for agricultural monitoring but remains persistently hindered by two fundamental challenges: limited inter-class separability arising from the high spectral-temporal similarity of co-occurring crops, and a label scarcity bottleneck exacerbated by the spatial non-stationarity of crop phenology. To address these limitations, this study proposes a novel Spatially-Adaptive Automated Sample Generation (SAASG) framework. By integrating multi-source remote sensing data with an iterative transfer learning strategy, SAASG autonomously generates high-fidelity training samples across heterogeneous landscapes. The framework’s core innovations are twofold. First, we engineer a Multi-source Phenological Feature Curve (MPFC) that synergizes the orthogonal information of Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) backscatter, the optical Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (NDVI), and a newly developed Contrast-Normalized Difference Vegetation Index (CNDVI). The CNDVI employs a novel spectro-structural modulation mechanism specifically designed to resolve late-season asymptotic saturation. Second, we introduce a Spatially-Adaptive Iterative Domain Adaptation mechanism utilizing a grid-based migration strategy. This discretizes the region into local domains to iteratively propagate phenological knowledge, effectively minimizing domain shift errors through spatial ensemble constraints. Demonstrated on peanuts in Shandong Province, China, the SAASG-generated samples exhibit superior phenological fidelity (Sequence Consistency Score = 0.982 ± 0.008; DTW distance = 0.172 ± 0.050) and possess a statistical distribution statistically congruent with in-situ ground-truth data. Leveraging these automatically labeled samples, we produced a 10-m resolution provincial peanut map with robust accuracy (Overall Accuracy > 0.85) across diverse agro-ecological zones. Crucially, a controlled substitution test confirmed that the classifier trained solely on SAASG samples achieved performance comparable to one trained on labor-intensive field data (ΔOA < 3%). These results confirm that the proposed framework provides a physically interpretable and operationally scalable solution to the training data crisis, enabling reliable large-scale mapping in regions with limited ground observations.

title: A multi-scale retrieval of three-dimensional ocean temperature by merging satellite and in situ observations
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Ocean temperature is a key variable in ocean dynamics, exerting broad impacts on the climate and ecosystems. In this study, we develop a multi-scale Bayesian hierarchical modeling framework to retrieve the three-dimensional (3D) ocean temperature by combining satellite and in situ observations. The retrieval process consists of two steps. The first step is to map the subsurface temperature anomaly ( T a ) relative to a climatological seasonal cycle based on satellite-measured sea surface temperature anomaly (SSTA) and sea surface height anomaly (SSHA). The mapping function is estimated from a geographically and seasonally varying coefficient (GSVC) linear regression model to capture the varying mapping relationship caused by the variations of ocean context with space and season. The second step is to fuse the mapped T a with in situ observations under a Bayesian hierarchical modeling framework. This allows the data fusion to take into consideration the mapping errors of T a due to not only variations of T a independent of SSTA and SSHA but also uncertainties in the estimated mapping function. The above mapping-fusion procedure is conducted separately on large-scale and mesoscale ocean processes to account for their distinct characteristics. Application of our method to the Indian Ocean sector of the Southern Ocean yields more accurate retrieval of 3D ocean temperature than a state-of-the-art data product, based on independent in situ test data.

title: FGPMamba: Frequency-geometry prior-guided Mamba for building change detection
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Building change detection (BCD) from high-resolution optical remote sensing imagery supports urban monitoring, land-use mapping, and construction progress assessment. However, in arid emerging-city environments, bare land, construction surfaces, concrete roofs, roads, and shadows may resemble changed buildings, resulting in pseudo changes, incomplete regions, and uncertain boundaries. This study proposes a frequency-geometry prior-guided Mamba network (FGPMamba) that combines global context modeling, phase-preserving frequency-domain feature recalibration, gradient-guided global–local fusion, and absolute-difference-based gradient refinement to exploit structural and boundary cues under appearance ambiguity. We also construct the African Desert Emerging-City Building Change Detection dataset (ADEC-CD) using 2018 and 2024 SuperView-2 imagery of Egypt’s New Administrative Capital. ADEC-CD adopts a geographically independent multi-zone split to reduce spatial leakage. On its geographically held-out test set, FGPMamba achieves mean F1, I o U 1 , Kappa, B-F1, and B-IoU scores of 87.49%, 77.76%, 86.70%, 64.78%, and 40.25%, respectively, over three independent runs. Under dataset-specific training and evaluation, FGPMamba also achieves the highest F1, B-F1, and B-IoU scores among the compared methods on SYSU-CD and HRCUS-CD. Controlled comparisons and feature-response analyses show that the proposed design improves pseudo-change suppression, changed-region completeness, and boundary reliability through frequency-dependent recalibration and boundary-concentrated refinement. These results indicate the potential of FGPMamba for construction monitoring in the study area and potentially similar arid environments. The code and dataset will be publicly available at: https://github.com/zjd1836/FGPMamba .

title: G2S2-IR: Glocal Gaussian Splatting with Surface Awareness for Inverse Rendering
Exploring the temporal consistency for point-level weakly-supervised temporal action localization
abstract: Point-supervised Temporal Action Localization (PTAL) adopts a lightly frame-annotated paradigm ( i.e. , labeling only a single frame per action instance) to train a model to effectively locate action instances within untrimmed videos. Most existing approaches design the task head of models with only a point-supervised snippet-level classification, without explicit modeling of understanding temporal relationships among frames of an action. However, understanding the temporal relationships of frames is crucial because it can help a model understand how an action is defined and therefore benefits the localization of complete action instances. To this end, in this paper, we design a multi-task learning framework that fully utilizes point supervision to boost the model’s temporal understanding capability for action localization. Specifically, we design three self-supervised temporal understanding tasks: (i) Action Completion, (ii) Action Order Understanding, and (iii) Action Regularity Understanding. These tasks help a model understand the temporal consistency of actions across videos. To the best of our knowledge, this is the first attempt to explicitly explore temporal consistency for point-supervision action localization. Extensive experimental results on four benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of the proposed method compared to several state-of-the-art approaches.

Geometry-aware dynamic convolutional network for instance-level segmentation of Martian landforms from high-resolution Digital Elevation Model-derived point clouds
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Analysis and interpretation of Martian surface landforms is one of the key topics in deep-space research, offering insights into the planet’s geological evolution and history of water activity. Automated extraction of Martian landforms can greatly assist researchers in rapidly locating and analyzing regions of interest. Therefore, instance segmentation based on remote sensing data represents a promising direction for automation in planetary science. To address the challenges of indistinct landform boundaries and over-segmentation in Martian remote sensing scenes, we propose an end-to-end 3D deep learning instance segmentation framework based on dynamic convolution. In this framework, we incorporate geometric information prediction of Martian landforms to enhance the network’s perception of morphological characteristics, bluewhich improves the separation of adjacent same-class instances. During training, we introduce two feature-space constraints-“pull” and “push” forces-to reduce intra-instance variance while increasing inter-instance separability. The proposed geometry-aware dynamic convolution framework is evaluated on a self-constructed water-formed landform dataset, an impact crater dataset, and a rock dataset from Mars rover perspective and achieves AP of 41.9 ± 0.1%, 63.7 ± 0.3%, and 68.6 ± 0.2%, remaining competitive with recent transformer-based methods such as Mask3D while outperforming clustering- and dynamic-convolution-based baselines. This end-to-end framework provides valuable technical support for subsequent geomorphological interpretation and potential exploration on Mars.

Sentinel-1 operational DInSAR services for surface displacements monitoring of the Italian territory through the P-SBAS processing chain: a review after 10 years of observations and data processing
Validation of TROPOMI SIF products based on spatial representativeness grading and atmospheric-geometric effect assessment
abstract: Satellite solar-induced chlorophyll fluorescence (SIF) is important for carbon cycle research, but its direct validation is often hindered by spatial scale mismatch between satellite footprints and in situ measurements. We developed a quantitative spatial representativeness grading framework for in situ SIF measurements. The framework uses two proxy metrics, the consistency index ( 𝐶 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 ) and relative absolute error ( 𝑅 𝐴 ⁢ 𝐸 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 ), to diagnose local SIF simulation consistency and point-to-footprint deviation. Using 6240 HyPlant pseudo-point/footprint samples, a domain-level threshold search yielded Level 1 criteria of 𝐶 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 ∈ [ 0 . 4 , 1 . 0 ] and 𝑅 𝐴 ⁢ 𝐸 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 ≤ 0 . 4 . Samples with the same 𝐶 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 range but 𝑅 𝐴 ⁢ 𝐸 𝑠 𝑖 𝑚 > 0 . 4 were classified as Level 2 and required upscaling. We applied this framework to 28 global sites to evaluate three TROPOMI SIF products using Sentinel-2 and ERA5-Land inputs. The framework retained 41–42% of the original matched samples. After controlling spatial scale effects, validation R 2 increased from 0.19 to 0.31 for TROPOSIF 735 and from 0.44 to 0.69 for both TROPOSIF 743 and TROPOSIF Caltech . Sensitivity analyses showed that this improvement was generally preserved under alternative tolerance thresholds and reference confidence criteria, although the proxy thresholds remain empirical. We further assessed cloud and sun-sensor geometry effects. TROPOSIF 735 was sensitive to cloud contamination, whereas TROPOSIF 743 and TROPOSIF Caltech remained robust under moderate cloud cover. Under clear skies, retrieval accuracy declined when solar zenith angle (SZA) exceeded 60 ° , while viewing zenith angle effects were limited after excluding large-SZA observations. Phase angle mismatch introduced systematic bias through canopy SIF anisotropy. Overall, this framework improves direct validation reliability and provides practical guidance for evaluating satellite SIF products.

title: Physics-informed machine learning for cloud detection
abstract: Accurate cloud detection is a critical preprocessing step for analyzing optical remote sensing data, such as from Landsat and Sentinel-2. In this study, we developed Fmask 5 (Version 5 of Function of mask) for cloud detection in Landsats 4–9 (Landsat 4, 5, 7, 8, and 9) and Sentinel-2 (Sentinel-2 A, B, and C) imagery, based on a novel physics-informed machine learning (PIML) framework. This framework synergistically integrates physical rules with machine learning (ML) models, overcoming their respective limitations. Specifically, a base ML model first generates a preliminary cloud mask to adapt to the application of physical rules, determining the optimal combination of spectral tests and thresholds for that image. The resulting physical-rule-adapted mask serves as additional “localized” training data to fine-tune the ML model. For a global, independent validation dataset combining simple random and disagreement-stratified samples from over 600 images per sensor, Fmask 5 achieved overall accuracies of 93.46% for Landsats 8–9, 92.50% for Landsats 4–7, and 95.38% for Sentinel-2, representing improvements of 1.6–6.0 percentage points over Fmask 4. The Fmask 5 algorithm is CPU-efficient, making it suitable for large-scale operational processing.

title: PC2Mesh: Reconstruction of building polygonal meshes from airborne LiDAR point clouds
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Polygonal meshes provide a compact and flexible representation for 3D buildings, supporting a wide range of photogrammetric and geometric applications. However, reconstructing high-fidelity building polygon meshes from airborne LiDAR point clouds remains challenging due to the non-uniform and variable-sided nature of polygonal topology and the complexity of urban environments characterized by diverse building geometries, uneven point densities, and occlusions. In this paper, we present PC2Mesh, a learning-based method that reconstructs polygonal building meshes directly from airborne LiDAR point clouds. While existing approaches rely on primitive detection (e.g., City3D, Point2Poly) or employ separate networks for vertex and face generation (e.g., Point2building), our method employs a unified transformer-based architecture that jointly learns mesh geometry and topology within a shared representation space. By representing arbitrary-sided polygons as learned token sequences, the method enables holistic mesh generation without preprocessing or handcrafted priors. This end-to-end formulation mitigates error propagation across stages and enhances reconstruction fidelity and robustness. Comprehensive experiments on open-source datasets demonstrate that our proposed method consistently outperforms state-of-the-art approaches in geometric accuracy and visual fidelity. Our method improves Edge Precision (EP) and Edge Recall (ER) by 9.1% and 24.7%, respectively, on the Zurich dataset, and by 8.3% and 20.2% on the Tallinn dataset. It also achieves the lowest Mean Distance Error (MDE), Hausdorff Distance (HD), and Chamfer Distance (CD) on both datasets. The source code of this work is freely available at https://github.com/BestyHon/PC2Mesh .

title: Topology-preserving river vectorization via HydroSAM and differentiable graph optimization under coarse labels
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Accurate river-network extraction supports global hydrological management and environmental monitoring. Automated extraction from remote-sensing imagery remains challenging because river morphology is highly variable, fine tributaries have weak visual signals, canopy and infrastructure can obscure channels, and dense annotations are scarce or spatially incomplete. Conventional raster predictions can also be fragmented and lack structural continuity. We present HydroSAM, a three-stage framework for raster extraction and topology-aware vectorization. A frozen SAM 2 Hiera encoder is adapted with QV-LoRA and the proposed Directional Curvilinear Prior Injection (DCPI), while a gated Digital Elevation Model (DEM) branch contributes coarse-scale topographic context. Segmentation is produced in a zero-prompt setting by the native SAM 2 mask decoder. A graph-guided differentiable vectorization stage then converts probability maps into connected parametric river networks. We also present M2Hydro, a benchmark containing 7,947 high-resolution 4096 × 4096 source image-annotation pairs across China. In single-run tests, HydroSAM-MM attains an F1 of 0.6995 and clDice of 0.7753 on M2Hydro. The evaluations indicate that HydroSAM supports parameter-efficient adaptation and is more resilient to the evaluated cross-regional domain shift than the convolutional and Transformer baselines.

title: Thinking on maps: how foundation model agents explore, remember, and reason in map environments
abstract: Map environments provide a fundamental medium for representing spatial structure and supporting navigation, planning, and geographic analysis. Understanding how foundation model (FM) agents acquire, consolidate, and utilize spatial knowledge in such environments is therefore critical for enabling reliable map-based reasoning and applications. However, most existing evaluations assess spatial ability in passive and non-interactive settings, without requiring models to actively explore environments, accumulate observations, and progressively construct spatial knowledge. Consequently, how spatial knowledge is formed during exploration and used for reasoning remains poorly understood. In this paper, we propose an interactive evaluation framework to examine how FM agents explore, remember, and reason in symbolic map environments. Agents incrementally navigate partially observable grid-based maps composed of roads, intersections, and points of interest (POIs), receiving only local observations at each step. Spatial understanding is then evaluated through a suite of tasks, including direction judgement, distance estimation, proximity judgement, POI density recognition, and path planning. By systematically varying exploration strategies, memory representations, and reasoning schemes across multiple foundation models, we identify distinct functional roles of these components. Exploration mainly affects experience acquisition but has a limited influence on final reasoning accuracy. In contrast, memory representation plays a central role in consolidating spatial experience, with structured memories—particularly sequential and graph-based forms—substantially improving performance on structure-intensive tasks such as path planning. Reasoning schemes further shape how stored spatial knowledge is utilized, with advanced prompting strategies supporting stronger multi-step inference. We also observe performance saturation across model versions and scales beyond a certain capability threshold, suggesting that further gains in map-based spatial understanding may depend more on spatially specialized representations and reasoning mechanisms than on model scaling alone. Overall, this work advances process-oriented evaluation of spatial cognition in FM agents and offers practical insights for building more reliable map-based reasoning systems.

title: Assessing heat dome effects on forest dynamics in the Pacific Northwest using Planet imagery
abstract: Increasingly frequent extreme heat events are imposing significant stress on forest ecosystems, with implications for both forests and the organisms that depend on them. This study evaluated the effects of the June 2021 Pacific Northwest (PNW) heat dome (a prolonged high-pressure system that generated record-breaking temperatures) on forest canopy health and subsequent recovery within the conifer-dominated Ellsworth Creek Preserve in Washington State, USA, using high-resolution Planet Labs satellite imagery. We analyzed normalized difference vegetation index (NDVI) trends from spring through fall from 2017 to 2025 to identify canopy stress and quantify changes in canopy greenness. The experimental forest thinning treatments, designed to accelerate old-growth structural characteristics, allowed us to evaluate canopy responses relative to restoration treatments. Our results showed marked declines in the summer NDVI during and following the 2021 heat dome, indicating substantial canopy stress. These declines differed from patterns observed in preceding years and occurred across all forest treatments. Changes in seasonal NDVI dynamics were evident in the control, thinned, clearcut, and old-growth stands; however, pairwise comparisons showed limited differences among canopy types, indicating broadly similar patterns of NDVI suppression during extreme events. The NDVI trajectories during the four post-heat dome years suggested partial recovery in canopy greenness, although the variability among the treatments remained high and overall NDVI levels remained below Pre2021 conditions in some stands through 2024. The recovery trajectories differed modestly among treatments, but we found limited evidence that canopy density substantially altered either the magnitude of canopy suppression or the subsequent recovery trajectories. Overall, these findings demonstrate that extreme heat events can induce widespread canopy stress across forest types and suggest that canopy structure alone may have a limited influence on canopy-scale responses under extreme atmospheric conditions. These results provide insight for adaptive forest management strategies aimed at maintaining ecosystem function under increasingly extreme climatic conditions.

title: Open long-tailed sonar image recognition via sparsity-aware tail memory learning
FedImageCLIP: Adapting CLIP in heterogeneous federated learning via joint local classifiers and mutual learning
Reliability-aware feedback learning for scribble-supervised 3D multi-organ segmentation
Limited local classification performance but promising spatial transferability of AlphaEarth Foundations for crop mapping across thermal gradients
Evaluating spectral unmixing techniques using imaging spectroscopy data for retrieval of green, non-photosynthetic vegetation, and soil fractional cover
abstract: Estimates of fractional cover of green vegetation (GV), non-photosynthetic vegetation (NPV), and soil provide valuable information about the Earth system. As the new generation of Earth visible-to-shortwave infrared (VSWIR) imaging spectrometers take orbit, global fractional cover data will be obtainable with new and improved spectral unmixing algorithms. Using an ASD Field Spectrometer and the spectral line point intercept (SLPIT) method, we estimate fractional cover from field measurements to compare to contemporaneous airborne (Airborne Visible/Infrared Imaging Spectrometer; AVIRIS NG ) and spaceborne (Earth surface Mineral dust source InvesTigation; EMIT) imaging spectroscopy data. Field data were collected in multiple biomes in the US Southwest at 84 validation sites. We used EndMember Combination Monte Carlo (E(MC) 2 ) and Multiple-Endmember Spectral Mixture Analysis (MESMA) to derive fractional cover, two candidate spectral unmixing algorithms used by current (e.g., EMIT) and future imaging spectroscopy missions. Field data exhibited strong agreement between ground and spaceborne/airborne measurements. Our best spectral unmixing approach, E(MC) 2 , produced mean absolute error of ≤0.05 for NPV, GV, and soil with uncertainties ≤0.08 for all classes. We further investigated the performance of global vs. local endmember libraries and found that the global library outperformed the local endmember library. We investigated normalization techniques and their effectiveness with our ground and image fractions. Additionally, we calculated uncertainties from both ground and image fractions. Field results aligned well and within uncertainty predictions from previously reported simulation work. These findings support the use of E(MC) 2 to be used in current and future imaging spectroscopy missions.

title: Elevation-dependent regulation of alpine vegetation productivity by snow cover and grazing on the Tibetan Plateau under a warming–wetting climate
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Grassland productivity on the Tibetan Plateau (TP) is fundamental to regional carbon cycling and ecosystem functioning and is strongly regulated by snow dynamics and grazing under a changing climate. However, the mechanisms by which alpine grassland productivity responds to interacting climatic, cryospheric, and anthropogenic drivers remain poorly constrained. Here, we integrated long-term multi-source Earth observation data to quantify the spatiotemporal trends of grassland gross primary productivity (GPP) across the TP from 1982 to 2018 and examined the relationships between GPP and snow dynamics, climate, and grazing intensity, with an explicit emphasis on elevation-dependent controls. Our results reveal a pronounced nonlinear reorganization of GPP controls along elevation gradients, with a critical transition zone at mid-elevations (∼3500–4000 m). Within this zone, warming exerted the strongest positive association with GPP, while grazing intensity also showed a positive spatial association with GPP. In contrast, at higher elevations (>4500 m), snow dynamics emerged as dominant constraints on GPP. Structural equation modeling further indicates that snow cover duration showed the strongest negative total effect among the modeled environmental variables, whereas grazing intensity showed an elevation – dependent association with GPP, shifting from a positive spatial correlation at mid – elevations to a negative correlation at high elevations. Across all elevation zones, soil moisture-mediated pathways consistently exert stronger controls on GPP than soil temperature pathways, highlighting water availability as the more direct and dominant constraint on alpine grassland productivity. These findings demonstrate that elevation fundamentally regulates the spatial organization of ecosystem productivity controls on the TP and underscore the importance of explicitly accounting for cryosphere–biosphere–human interactions when assessing alpine carbon dynamics under a warming and wetting climate.

title: Active CO2 lidar extends satellite monitoring of urban fossil-fuel CO2 emissions to high-aerosol cities
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Cities with high aerosol loading are critical yet underserved targets for satellite-based monitoring of urban fossil-fuel CO 2 (ffCO 2 ) emissions, because passive XCO 2 retrievals often suffer from severe data loss and aerosol-induced uncertainty under polluted conditions. Here, we evaluate whether spaceborne active CO 2 lidar can extend satellite carbon monitoring to such observationally challenging environments. We combine CO 2 observations from the DQ-1 Aerosol and Carbon Dioxide Lidar (ACDL) with Sentinel-5P/TROPOMI NO 2 retrievals to construct an active–passive framework. Near-synchronous ACDL–TROPOMI overpasses are used to derive city-specific ffCO 2 -to-NO x emission ratios, which are then applied to TROPOMI-derived daily NO x emissions to reconstruct observation-constrained ffCO 2 variability. Among the top 100 urban ffCO 2 emitters, high-AOD cities are concentrated in the Asia–Pacific region, and under polluted conditions, DQ-1 provides 201.6% and 107.8% more effective CO 2 observations than OCO-2 and OCO-3, respectively. Applications to six high-AOD cities in North China and India reveal physically interpretable seasonal variability, with monthly emission magnitudes broadly consistent with EDGAR and ODIAC inventories (r = 0.79–0.81). These results demonstrate that active CO 2 lidar, when combined with dense NO 2 observations, can provide an independent top-down constraint to support urban carbon monitoring and mitigation assessment in polluted cities where passive carbon satellites are most limited.

title: Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning for Foundation Models
Retrieval of nighttime oceanic liquid cloud optical and microphysical parameters from VIIRS observations: a physics-informed machine learning approach
Piecewise log-normal modeling of Sentinel-1 co-cross polarization coherence and application to wind field Bayesian inversion
abstract: Accurate estimates of kilometer-scale ocean surface wind fields is critical for many applications, including weather forecasting, marine navigation, offshore wind energy development, and coastal risk management. Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) plays a key role in retrieving wind speed by analyzing changes in sea surface roughness, described through Geophysical Model Functions (GMFs). However, the inverse problem of wind retrieval from SAR data is under-determined, requiring ancillary information from Numerical Weather Models (NWP) to resolve ambiguities in the wind direction. The Co-Cross-Polarization Coherence (CCPC) has recently emerged as a valuable SAR-derived observation for improving wind direction estimates. While an initial GMF for CCPC has been proposed, it proved inadequate for high wind speeds. We present PGMF-2, a refined GMF for CCPC, ensuring reliable performance up to approximately 25 m/s by modeling its wind speed components as log-normal functions. The need for crosstalk calibration is mitigated by a burst-based processing. Monte Carlo simulations confirm that the unique odd-symmetry of the CCPC and the different impact of the wind direction modulation on its real and imaginary parts complements the Normalized Radar Cross Section (NRCS) to estimate the wind direction. This combination enables wind direction retrieval without NWP priors, even outperforming NWP-based inversions between 7 and 15 m/s. The Mean Absolute Error on direction reaches as low as 25 ∘ in favorable (in particular between 30 ∘ –90 ∘ and 270 ∘ –330 ∘ of wind direction relative to the satellite antenna, where the NRCS and the CCPC have overlapping wind direction variability) high-wind conditions. Co-observations with the HY-2B scatterometer, supplemented by a case study on Storm Alex (2020), serve as a proof of concept of the Bayesian scheme on real-world observations, successfully retrieving the typical flow organization of the cyclonic system without reliance on NWP priors.

title: Remote sensing of hydrothermal alteration in active volcanic environments: A critical review and integrated analysis of Lastarria volcano
abstract: Hydrothermal alteration is a key process in active volcanic systems, influencing edifice stability, fluid circulation, degassing pathways, and volcanic hazards. Remote sensing is widely used to map hydrothermal alteration; however, many approaches treat alteration-related surfaces as static targets, so their reliability, transferability, and process significance in active volcanic environments remain insufficiently evaluated. This study synthesizes commonly used remote sensing approaches and examines the behavior and interpretive implications of representative outputs at Lastarria volcano, which is an arid, high-altitude, vegetation-free system with active fumarolic fields. We compare visual interpretation, VNIR-SWIR reflectance products, pixel-based and sub-pixel mapping outputs, UAV thermal infrared observations, and LiDAR-derived surface-state information. The results show that visual interpretation, reflectance-based products, and pixel-based or sub-pixel outputs delineate broad alteration-related patterns, but their extent, internal structure, and interpretive meaning vary with methodological choices, surface mixing, and environmental surface states. Thermal infrared observations constrain apparent surface-temperature anomalies and fumarole-proximal activity, whereas LiDAR-derived products provide complementary information on surface state, morphology, and roughness. These observations do not converge on a single alteration representation; instead, they capture different aspects of the volcanic-hydrothermal system. Environmental, climatic, and surface controls, including exposure state, moisture, surface reworking, and seasonality, further limit direct transferability among volcanic settings. We suggest that remote sensing of hydrothermal alteration in active volcanic environments should move from deterministic mapping toward process-oriented and uncertainty-aware interpretation, with temporal persistence, spatial coherence, process plausibility, and independent support providing a basis for future multi-temporal analysis and monitoring.

title: DescribeEarth: Detailed localized captioning for remote sensing images
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Automated textual description of remote sensing images is crucial for unlocking their full potential in diverse applications, from environmental monitoring to urban planning and disaster management. However, existing studies in remote sensing image captioning primarily focus on the image level, lacking object-level fine-grained interpretation, which prevents the full utilization and transformation of the rich semantic and structural information contained in remote sensing images. Consequently, we propose Geo-DLC, a novel task for fine-grained object-level image captioning in remote sensing. To systematically establish and evaluate this new paradigm, we introduce a comprehensive suite encompassing a dataset, a benchmark, and a specialized model. Specifically, we construct DE-Dataset, a large-scale collection comprising 25 categories and 261,806 annotated instances with detailed descriptions of object attributes, relationships, and contexts. To provide a rigorous evaluation standard, we develop DE-Benchmark, an LLM-assisted evaluation protocol based on question answering, to accurately measure the capabilities of models on the Geo-DLC task. Furthermore, we present DescribeEarth, an MLLM architecture explicitly tailored for this task. It integrates a scale-adaptive focal strategy and a domain-guided fusion module, which leverage the features of remote sensing Vision-Language Model (VLM) to encode high-resolution details and category priors while maintaining the global context. Extensive evaluations show that DescribeEarth achieves the highest aggregate scores on the simple and complex subsets and matches GPT-4o on the out-of-distribution subset of DE-Benchmark. Its clearest gains occur in surrounding-context coverage and in categories whose interpretation depends strongly on overhead spatial layout and remote-sensing context. All data, code, and weights are publicly available at https://github.com/earth-insights/DescribeEarth .

title: 160 Years of Etna summit craters through a photogrammetry-based time machine
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: This study presents a quantitative, multi-temporal assessment of Etna’s summit morpho-structural evolution, spanning a 160-year (1865–2024) period. We integrated historical topographic maps with modern, high-resolution remote sensing data, including Unoccupied Aerial System surveys. Dataset-specific validation and statistical error propagation yielded root mean square errors ranging from decametric values for the earliest cartographic sources to metric values for the post-2020 datasets. The resulting topographic time series was interpreted alongside geological observations and previously published geodetic analyses. This integrated reconstruction documents the transition from a predominantly monocentric summit configuration to a highly dynamic polycentric system, and reveals contrasting morpho-structural behaviours among the four summit craters. VOR is characterized by recent constructive growth, BN and NEC by recurrent infilling followed by subsidence, whereas the SEC exhibits persistent constructive growth accompanied by progressive eastward expansion. These differences are consistent with variations in crater position, structural setting, shallow feeding-system configuration, and dominant eruptive style. The long-term evolution of the summit area is also consistent with the influence of the North-East and South Rift zones, and with published geodetic observations describing the seaward deformation of Etna’s eastern flank. Overall, the reconstructed evolution highlights the interaction between volcanic construction, structural controls, and gravitational deformation in shaping a continuously changing and asymmetric summit system. The proposed geospatial workflow provides a reproducible and transferable framework for integrating heterogeneous historical and modern topographic datasets and for investigating long-term morpho-structural change at other highly active volcanoes.

title: Atmospheric restoration is a prerequisite for sub-pixel fire mapping: A smoke-robust protocol across five fire regions
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Wildfires exert profound impacts on global ecosystems; however, accurate satellite-based burn area extraction is frequently confounded by the inherent mixed-pixel issue and complex atmospheric conditions. Although sub-pixel mapping (SPM) can resolve the mixed pixel issue, the extent to which its extraction accuracy depends on initial atmospheric preprocessing under diverse haze and smoke conditions remains poorly quantified. Furthermore, the conditions under which such preprocessing remains effective, and the boundary of its operational envelope, are not well understood. This study introduces a Smoke-Robust Sub-pixel Mapping (SRSPM) protocol to systematically diagnose atmospheric preprocessing efficacy prior to SPM. Using both simulated and real atmospheric states across five distinct fire regions, we systematically evaluate the sensitivity of sub-pixel fire perimeter delineation to different levels of haze contamination. Our findings demonstrate that atmospheric scattering inherently degrades the spatial allocation capabilities of SPM, leading to severe omission errors. Restoring contaminated spectral signals is shown to be essential, rather than merely beneficial, for accurate mapping when haze contamination is substantial. Crucially, our quantitative diagnosis reveals the operational limits of the SRSPM protocol: the dehazing benefit grows with haze intensity and remains substantial up to the strongest simulated contamination ( w = 1); in one region it turns positive only beyond w ≈0.73, delineating the quantitative envelope of the SRSPM protocol. Overall, this work establishes the SRSPM protocol as a practical diagnostic tool for quantifying the interaction between atmospheric correction and sub-pixel spatial allocation, providing empirical guidance for operational disaster monitoring in complex atmospheric environments.

title: Improving automatic glacier mapping accuracy, robustness, and reliability across the Third Pole Region
abstract: Most automatic glacier mapping methods applied in the Third Pole Region (TPR), exhibit suboptimal accuracy for debris-covered glaciers, high sensitivity to interferences, and large uncertainty in model outputs, thereby limiting their operational utility. These challenges can be mitigated by deploying advanced deep learning models and enhancing dataset representativeness across complex imaging conditions. Accordingly, we compiled three large-scale datasets used for model development, glacier-level mapping evaluation, and cross-sensor generalisation assessment, respectively. We then evaluated several state-of-the-art deep learning networks and found that the adapted TransUNet performed best. On the test dataset, the model achieves a glacier Intersection over Union (IoU) of 90% and 83% in patches featuring debris-free and debris-covered glaciers, respectively, while maintaining robust under challenging conditions. Glacier-level validation further confirms the effective detection of glacier counts and precise outlines, with both metrics improving with glacier area and the global IoUTPR > 80%. Uncertainty quantification shows high output reliability, with expected calibration errors of 0.029 and 0.009 for the test and glacier-level test datasets, respectively. Our fully automated 2024–2025 Karakoram glacier inventory, comprising 12,981 glaciers covering a total area of ~19,484 km2, exhibits high agreement with earlier inventories and reflects current glacier state. The primary contribution of this study is the development of a scalable framework that, by optimising dataset representativeness and algorithmic architectures, significantly elevates the accuracy, robustness, reliability and operational value of glacier mapping across the TPR.

title: Fusing SAR and SWIM observations to improve the global stokes drift estimates
abstract: Stokes drift of ocean surface waves is an important quantity in wave-current coupling theories that affects the dynamics and tracer transport in the upper ocean. However, direct measurement of Stokes drift is elusive. More commonly, it is computed from measured wave spectrum. While in situ measurements of wave spectrum are available from wave buoys, they are mostly limited to coastal regions. Remote sensing of wave spectrum by the Synthetic Aperture Radar (SAR) or the Surface Wave Investigation and Monitoring (SWIM) instrument enables wave spectrum observations globally. Yet both systems present distinct constraints: SAR provides directional information but suffers from velocity bunching effects that restrict measurable wavenumbers and cause spectral distortions, while SWIM offers broader spectral coverage with minimal amplitude underestimation but produces directionally ambiguous spectra. To address these complementary limitations, we propose a novel fusion framework to combine SAR and SWIM using conventional signal processing techniques. We validate the fused Stokes drift against in situ wave buoy measurements at Ocean Station Papa, Southeast Hawaii, and Southern Ocean Flux Station. Compared to the standalone SAR and SWIM results, our fusion approach improves Stokes drift estimates and demonstrates robust performance for the mean Stokes drift vector across various sea states. In addition, we categorize the error sources of the fusion approach into distinct types to guide future improvements. Finally, we apply this fusion approach to the global ocean, which yields seasonal Stokes drift estimates that are more consistent with the established understanding of global wave patterns than estimates based on SWIM alone. These findings show the potential of the fusion approach toward an improved estimate of global Stokes drift.

title: WISE: A lightweight, weakly-supervised model for onboard fire smoke detection and localization
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Wildfire smoke detection from satellite imagery is critical for early warning and rapid response. For onboard satellite deployment, detection systems must operate under strict memory and latency constraints while providing spatially informative outputs for downstream decision-making. Existing tile-level classification methods are computationally efficient but lack spatial localization, whereas pixel-level segmentation approaches provide detailed masks yet are typically too computationally demanding for real-time onboard execution. To address this gap, we propose WISE (Weakly-supervised Inference-efficient Smoke Extraction), a deployment-oriented framework for onboard fire smoke detection and localization. WISE leverages only tile-level annotations through a teacher–student distillation strategy, where an offline teacher provides soft spatial supervision to a lightweight WISE-Student optimized for efficient onboard inference. The student jointly predicts tile-level smoke presence and smoke probability maps within a single forward pass, enabling spatially informative detection under strict computational constraints. WISE was evaluated through in-orbit execution aboard the ISS-mounted IMAGIN-e payload. Three model variants achieve average inference times of 0.10 s, 0.14 s, and 0.26 s per tile, indicating near-real-time per-tile inference within onboard resource limits. Ground-based experiments on Landsat 5 and Landsat 8 imagery further indicate effective detection and spatially informative localization. The best-performing variant achieves a mean tile-level F1 score of 0.964 and a mean pixel-level F1 score of 0.750 across 10 runs, while containing only 0.12M parameters and requiring approximately 3 GFLOPs. Together, these results indicate that WISE is a practical candidate for low-latency wildfire smoke monitoring from space under onboard resource constraints.

title: A multi-sensor and multi-temporal GeoAI framework for resolving ecological scale mismatch in Antarctica
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Advances in remote sensing (RS) and artificial intelligence (AI) are enabling new approaches to ecological monitoring across spatial and temporal scales. However, vegetation mapping in polar environments remains constrained by a fundamental mismatch between the fine spatial scale of ecological processes and the coarse resolution of satellite observations, as well as by limited availability of biologically reliable training data. In this study, we address these challenges by developing an end-to-end GeoAI framework that integrates field observations, drone imagery, and satellite time-series data to enable cross-scale vegetation mapping. We propose a progressive weak-to-strong labelling workflow that begins with 1) biologically grounded quadrat annotations, to create iteratively expanded training data along with 2) spectral similarity combined with machine learning, followed by 3) training with deep learning (DL) models for pixel-level segmentation. Native Sentinel-2 observations (10–20 m spatial resolution) were processed using DL-based super-resolution to an approximately 1 m output grid. High-resolution drone DL predictions were subsequently transformed into fractional cover labels aligned to the super-resolved satellite grid, supporting cross-scale modelling across centimetre-to-metre resolutions. We evaluate multiple DL architectures using spatially separated UAV evaluation data and assess satellite-scale performance as agreement with UAV-derived fractional cover reference labels. Our results demonstrate that the proposed framework substantially improves the scalability and ecological relevance of vegetation mapping in data-limited environments. The best-performing drone-scale DL model (DeepLabv3+) achieved an overall accuracy of 0.91 and a Macro-F1 score of 0.85 for fine-scale vegetation segmentation. At the satellite scale, the U-Net fractional-cover model achieved strong predictive performance for dominant vegetation classes, including cyanobacteria (R 2 = 0.94) and red Hennediella heimii moss (R 2 = 0.88), with reduced performance for spectrally complex or sparsely represented classes, demonstrating effective cross-scale vegetation mapping despite challenges associated with sub-pixel heterogeneity and spectral mixing. This study provides a generalisable methodological framework for integrating multi-sensor data and AI in ecological RS, demonstrating strong cross-scale performance while illustrating the challenges of capturing fine-scale vegetation heterogeneity at satellite scales.

title: Extending ocean color product to three dimensions assisted by high spectral resolution lidar data
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Satellite ocean color remote sensing has revolutionized our understanding of global marine ecosystems, but remains fundamentally limited to two-dimensional (2D) observations. To address this limitation, we propose a Depth-Resolved Generalized Inherent Optical Property (DR-GIOP) model that merges passive multispectral remote sensing reflectance ( R rs ) from MODIS-Aqua with active depth-resolved particulate backscattering profiles ( b bp ) from High Spectral Resolution Lidar (HSRL). Using lidar derived b bp ( z ) at a single wavelength and ocean color sensor derived spectral R rs ( λ ) as inputs, the model solves for depth-resolved spectral non-water absorption a pg ( z , λ ), particulate backscattering b bp ( z , λ ), and chlorophyll-a concentration Chl ( z ). We validated this model using coincident MODIS, airborne HSRL, and shipborne in-situ measurements from the SABOR campaign and three NAAMES campaigns. The results demonstrate that DR-GIOP successfully reconstructs reasonable three-dimensional (3D) optical structures, achieving the correlation coefficient r =∼0.85 for a pg ( z , λ ), b bp ( z , λ ), and Chl ( z ).Comparative analysis indicates that DR-GIOP significantly outperforms traditional 2D models such as Seeded GIOP, GIOP-DC, and QAA. Furthermore, we quantitatively analyze the shallow-layer bias of passive 2D remote sensing and demonstrate how active–passive fusion effectively mitigates this bias. This study proposes a promising framework for 3D ocean color reconstruction, offering new insights for future multi-sensor satellite missions. In the future, we can envision the realization of a satellite that carries an advanced HSRL and multi-spectral sensors, providing high accuracy of b bp ( z ) and R rs ( λ ) and promising 3D ocean subsurface observations at a global scale.

title: Bridging cloud-induced gaps in MODIS leaf area index products using high-frequency geostationary satellite observations
venue: International Journal of Applied Earth Observation and Geoinformation
abstract: Leaf Area Index (LAI) is a fundamental variable for characterizing vegetation canopy structure and ecosystem functioning. However, persistent cloud contamination substantially constrains the spatiotemporal continuity of LAI products derived from polar-orbiting satellite observations. In contrast, geostationary satellites provide dense temporal sampling, offering a valuable observational basis for filling data gaps in polar-orbiting satellite products. To bridge this observational gap, this study develops an observation-complementary framework that integrates high-frequency Himawari-8 Advanced Himawari Imager (AHI) observations with MODIS LAI products to achieve LAI reconstruction in cloud-prone regions. Within this framework, AHI observations are first used to retrieve LAI at a spatial resolution of 2 km using a Random Forest model trained with a high-quality MODIS-based benchmark dataset, and are then downscaled to 500 m using MODIS-derived spatial texture information. The reconstructed AHI LAI is subsequently integrated into low-quality or missing MODIS pixels to generate a fused AHI-MODIS LAI dataset over China. Validation against in-situ measurements and cross-comparison results show that the fused product maintains reasonable numerical consistency and stable temporal trajectories. Data availability increases from 70.70% to 90.90% under the 4-day compositing cycle. These results indicate that geostationary-polar-orbiting observation complementarity provides a practical pathway for improving the continuity and usability of optical LAI products in persistently cloudy regions, while remaining subject to the constraints of optical observations and cross-scale reconstruction assumptions.

title: BD-Diff: Generative Diffusion Model for Image Deblurring on Unknown Domains with Blur-Decoupled Learning
TAME-MA: Taming Mobile Agents via Trajectory-Level Trustworthiness Under Jailbreak Manipulations
PosePAL: Efficient Animal Pose Labeling Using Point Trackers
abstract: Abstract Automatically estimating animal poses from videos is important for studying animal behavior. Existing methods do not perform reliably, partly because they rely on high-quality training data, and existing such datasets are small. It is challenging and expensive to create such data, due to the large variations in animal morphology and the difficulty of frame-wise video annotation in general. In this paper, we introduce an animal pose labeling pipeline that leverages test-time optimization of a point tracker, providing temporally-consistent annotations at low cost. Given a video, we fine-tune a lightweight appearance embedding inside a pre-trained general-purpose point tracker on a sparse set of annotated frames. These annotations can be obtained from human labelers or off-the-shelf pose detectors. The fine-tuned model is then applied to the rest of the frames for automatic labeling. Our method achieves state-of-the-art performance at a reasonable annotation cost. We believe our pipeline offers a valuable tool for the automatic quantification of animal behavior. Visit our project webpage at https://zhuoyang-pan.github.io/animal-labeling .

title: Voxelized 3D Gaussian Representation for Dense Visual SLAM on Embedded Vision System
Pseudo-label Refinement and Model-State Recovery for Continual Test-Time Adaptation on Semantic Segmentation
Sampling-Free Universal Domain Adaptive Object Detection with Synergistic Optimization Alignment
abstract: Abstract Universal Domain Adaptive Object Detection (UniDAOD) addresses domain shifts in open-world scenarios without assuming pre-defined shared categories between source and target domains. Despite progress in this field, existing methods rely heavily on thresholding techniques to filter private category samples, which introduces challenges in hyperparameter tuning and handling noisy data. To overcome these limitations, we propose Synergistic Optimization Alignment (SOA), a sampling-free framework that tackles two challenges inherent in UniDAOD: multi-scale discriminator discrepancy and task-dominant gradient conflict. To address the discrepancy among multi-scale discriminators, we propose Multi-Scale Discriminator Alignment (MDA) to adaptively aggregate under-aligned discriminators for shared classes, ensuring consistent feature alignment across scales. To address task-dominant gradient conflicts, we propose Gradient Coordinated Optimization (GCO), which suppresses conflicting domain-alignment gradients and coordinates their magnitudes to prevent domain over-alignment, thereby mitigating private-class interference while preserving beneficial domain-invariant supervision. Extensive experiments on open-set, partial-set, and closed-set domain adaptation benchmarks demonstrate that SOA outperforms state-of-the-art UniDAOD and DAOD methods. Code is available at https://github.com/zyfone/SOA .

title: Mapping rodent-induced disturbance of biological soil crusts using PlanetScope imagery and deep-learning-informed graph cut
abstract: Biological soil crusts (biocrusts) function as a “living skin” at the soil–atmosphere interface and provide important ecosystem services in drylands. While climate change and anthropogenic disturbances are well-recognized drivers of biocrust degradation, mechanical disturbance by wildlife remains poorly understood. Burrowing rodents can directly damage biocrusts by excavating and displacing soil, creating bright disturbance patches that contrast sharply with the darker surrounding biocrust matrix. Based on this brightness contrast, we developed a mapping framework using high-resolution PlanetScope basemaps from 2017 to 2025 to delineate rodent-induced biocrust disturbance in the Gurbantunggut Desert, China. The framework follows a two-stage strategy. First, a Swin-UPerNet model generates colony probability maps to capture diverse colony patterns. Second, these maps are refined using a morphology-based scoring scheme to enhance small and weakly expressed patches, and then optimized by graph cut using brightness-gradient information to sharpen boundaries. Validation against 125 independent field-supported reference sites showed that the framework achieved an overall accuracy (OA) of 97.52% (97.10–97.92%), with an F1-score of 0.804 (0.778–0.826) and an intersection over union (IoU) of 0.672 (0.636–0.703) for the disturbance class. Rodent-induced disturbance was spatially extensive, reaching 1218.34 km 2 (1157.87–1284.25 km 2 ) in 2019 and comprising approximately 1.11 million mapped disturbance patches. This mapped footprint was equivalent to 10.3% of the estimated fractional biocrust-cover area for that year, indicating that rodent excavation occupied a substantial area that could otherwise support biocrust cover. The extent of mapped disturbance was highly dynamic over time, declining sharply through 2022, reaching a minimum in 2023, and then rebounding rapidly through 2025. Representative trajectories further suggest that rodent-induced disturbance can expand rapidly and persist for years, and that its dynamics may be coupled with hydroclimatic stress in biocrust-covered landscapes. These findings highlight rodent-induced disturbance as an important yet underrecognized component of desert ecosystem dynamics and provide a remote-sensing framework for monitoring such disturbances under a changing climate.

title: Can AlphaEarth foundations redefine the paradigm of gridded population mapping? A systematic evaluation across 18 global cities and large-scale mapping applications
Spatiotemporal extension of all-sky downward shortwave radiation over mountainous area
abstract: Surface downward shortwave radiation (DSR) is a key component in the radiation budget, yet mountainous regions remain challenging due to complex topographic effects. The pronounced spatial heterogeneity of DSR in these areas complicates validation, as direct site-based observations are generally not representative of kilometer-scale satellite or reanalysis products. To address this issue, this study proposes a spatiotemporal extension method for all-sky downward shortwave radiation over mountainous areas (STEMAR). First, a linear all-sky radiative transfer model for rugged terrain was developed. By leveraging time-for-space substitution and the regional cloud hypothesis, the model can accurately map daily DSR over rugged terrain at a 30 m × 30 m resolution with at least three radiation sites and an all-sky imager. When ground-based cloud observations are unavailable, the model can be simplified into a two-component formulation, requiring only two radiation sites. The Copernicus DEM and Sentinel-2 L2A surface albedo were used to calculate the topographic factors and multiple scattering among adjacent terrain grids. The main validation was based on 53 days of observations collected at Saihanba Mechanical Forest Farm, Hebei Province, China, from August to September 2022. An additional 56 days of observations from April to May 2022 were used to test performance during a second seasonal period at the same sites. The RMSE values were 26.4 W/m 2 and 5.3 W/m 2 for hourly and daily DSR, respectively, with corresponding biases below 2.4 W/m 2 and 1.1 W/m 2 . STEMAR is expected to serve as a reference approach for obtaining ground-truth values to validate daily DSR products in mountainous area.

title: Nested generative downscaling of passive microwave satellite data for navigation-scale Arctic sea ice forecasting
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Rapid Arctic sea ice decline is increasing the accessibility of high-latitude shipping routes, but route-scale planning remains limited by the spatial resolution and ice-edge accuracy of Arctic sea ice concentration (SIC) forecasts. Coarse forecast products can smooth marginal ice zones, narrow straits, and fine-scale ice-edge features that are important for identifying navigable corridors during seasonal melt and freeze-up. Here we introduce IceNest, a navigation-oriented Arctic SIC forecasting framework that generates daily 6.25 km SIC forecasts up to 30 days ahead. IceNest couples a deep learning-based 25 km pan-Arctic forecast ensemble with a conditional diffusion model for residual downscaling. The forecasting ensemble uses the long OSI SAF SSM/I(S) passive microwave record together with historical environmental variables from ERA5, while the downscaling model learns AMSR-scale residual corrections from AMSR-series observations. Across 2020–2023, IceNest outperformed damped persistence and the evaluated Copernicus Climate Change Service seasonal forecast systems in terms of binary accuracy and integrated ice-edge error, with the largest gains during summer melt and autumn freeze-up. Route simulations along the Northeast Passage further yielded smaller errors in navigable-window timing and route distance than GloSea5/6 when evaluated against an AMSR2-based reference, highlighting the framework’s relevance to Arctic transit planning.

title: HELIOS-Net: Hourly daytime estimation of land surface temperature with integration of observational solar-cloud-satellite geometry and deep neural network
venue: ISPRS Journal of Photogrammetry and Remote Sensing
abstract: Geostationary satellite-based land surface temperature (LST) is vital for monitoring diurnal thermal dynamics owing to its extensive spatial coverage and high temporal resolution.
